newsitem.title: ITALY: OLYMPICS-ITALY CHEERS INITIAL ROME VERDICT.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ITALY CHEERS INITIAL ROME VERDICT.

text.p: Italy greeted the International Olympic Committee's positive evaluation of its 2004 Games bid for Rome as proof the city is close to clearing its first Olympic hurdle.
"The IOC has decided -- Rome goes through," cheered Rome daily La Repubblica after the Committee issued a report elevating Rome and Athens to front-runners in the race.
Five of the 11 cities vying for the Games will be short-listed on March 7 and the winner named on September 5.
"I have to say that the report on Rome is excellent, better than could have been expected," said Primo Nebiolo, Italian president of the International Amateur Athletic Federation.
"Now we know that the candidacy is serious and very valid," added Nebiolo, an IOC member.

Rome mayor Francesco Rutelli, who has championed the Olympic cause despite protests that The Eternal City was now too chaotic and traffic-clogged to stage an event of such magnitude, said the IOC had immediately recognised the calibre of its bid.
"Rome has presented a complete, in-depth, incisive dossier and the Committee immediately appreciated it," he said.
"A victory for Rome would above all be a victory for Italy, for its image, its sport and its organisational skills."

The IOC report praised high local support for Rome's bid, excellent and professional plans including some venues in historic locations, thorough preparations for the athletes' village and accommodation and apparently high revenues.
But it said traffic was a major problem, although improvements were planned.
Raffaele Ranucci, who is leading the bid, said he was delighted by the assessment but Rome could not afford to "rest on its laurels". The city last staged the Games in 1960.
Italian Olympic Committee president Mario Pescante said he had been sure all along Rome's bid would be applauded.
But he warned: "This is the first step, the easiest one. Things start to get tougher now."
Opponents of Rome's candidacy have vowed there will be no let-up in their campaign to block the bid and accused officials of lying about how they would pay for the Olympics.

"We're not surprised by (the IOC's) evaluation as it was based on superficial and falsely construed data provided by the bid's organising committee," said Cristiano Brughita, spokesman for the Committee Against the Olympics in Rome.
The Committee is made up of hundreds of intellectuals and environmentalists who say the Games would be costly, disruptive and environmentally harmful to the ancient city.
Brughita said his group, which has asked to meet IOC chief Juan Antonio Samaranch to discuss the matter, had sent a dossier to the IOC detailing "the falsehoods".

"In particular, we underscored the financial instability of the Rome bid and the uncertainty of promises made by the state since they were made by neither the government nor approved by parliament," he said.

The government has pledged $1.7 billion for sports facilities and other building project if Rome's bid beats those from Cape Town, Buenos Aires, Istanbul, Lille, Rio de Janeiro, San Juan, Stockholm, Seville, Athens and St Petersburg.

Promoters have promised that Rome would undergo a major facelift to be ready for the Games, including major improvements to its choked traffic system such as a new third lane along the city's ring road reserved for Olympic traffic.
